extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy (Kantian teleology / Critique of Judgment)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Kant's criteria for when and how to judge natural objects as purposive (teleology), including the distinction between reflective and determinant judgement, regulative vs constitutive principles, and the competing systems (idealism vs realism) about purposiveness. Useful for philosophical analysis of teleology and methodological guidance for natural science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judging as a natural purpose by internal form versus asserting a purpose of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: To judge of a thing as a natural purpose on account of its internal form is very different from taking the existence of that thing to be a purpose of nature; the former requires only the concept of a possible purpose, the latter requires knowledge of the final purpose (scopus) of nature and a reference to something supersensible beyond nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internal organisation (e.g., the form of a blade of grass) suffices to show that its origin is possible according to the rule of purposes for our faculty of judgement. But to assert that the thing exists as a purpose of nature requires going beyond natural teleological knowledge to a supersensible ground; treat internal purposiveness as a methodological indicator, not as metaphysical proof of final ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: External purposive relations are only hypothetically purposive
rubrics_metrics.description: When we judge purposiveness from externally purposive references (how things are used by other beings), we arrive at no categorical purpose: such purposive reference rests on ever more distant conditions and so cannot establish natural purposes categorically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (grass → ox → man) show that external chains of use do not justify calling something a natural purpose; avoid treating instrumental relations as evidence of an intrinsic teleological end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organisation (matter organised) entails the concept of natural purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Only insofar as matter is organised does it necessarily carry with it the concept of a natural purpose, because specific form is at the same time a product of nature; this leads to the Idea of nature as a system in accordance with the rule of purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the concept of purposiveness when encountering organised beings as a heuristic for investigating their constitution; recognise this as a regulative expectation (principle of Reason) rather than a constitutive metaphysical claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of Reason as a regulative maxim (everything good for something)
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of Reason in teleological reflection is: 'everything in the World is some way good for something; nothing is vain in it.' This is a subjective principle or maxim to guide reflective judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply it as a regulative principle to seek system-wide purposiveness in nature to guide inquiry, but do not treat it as establishing objective, constitutive laws of nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teleology is regulative not constitutive for natural science
rubrics_metrics.description: Teleological judgement provides a clue for considering natural things in reference to an already given ground of determination according to a new rule (final causes), but it is not a constitutive principle of natural science and does not supplant mechanical causality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use teleological reflection to supplement mechanistic inquiry where mechanistic explanation is inadequate, without prejudicing mechanical causality or making teleology an ontological claim about natural causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mixing natural science and theology (domestic vs foreign principles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sciences may be based on domestic (internal) principles or borrow foreign (peregrina) concepts from other sciences. Introducing the concept of God as an internal principle of natural science creates circularity and confuses the boundaries between natural science and theology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep natural scientific explanations within principles that can be empirical or belong to the science itself; if you use theological concepts, mark them as foreign auxiliaries and avoid dogmatically importing them into natural science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible teleological language is analogical/metaphorical, not literal design attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: In teleology (as referred to Physics) we may speak of the wisdom, economy, forethought, beneficence of Nature, but only analogically: the word 'design' expresses a principle of the reflective, not the determinant, judgement and must not introduce a supernatural cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use teleological terminology as heuristic analogies derived from our own technical Reason; explicitly avoid asserting that inanimate matter literally has intentions or that a superior Architect is thereby proven.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physics should restrict itself to mechanisms it can replicate (propaedeutic role of teleology)
rubrics_metrics.description: Teleology usually forms no proper part of theoretical natural science but serves as a propaedeutic or transition to theology because organisation surpasses human art and physics can only treat what can be subjected to observation or experiment and be produced by similar laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When studying organised nature, pursue mechanistic, reproducible explanations as far as possible; use teleological reflection only as a guide when mechanistic reproduction fails or is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflective versus determinant Judgement distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: The determinant Judgement subsumes under given laws or concepts and has no autonomy; the reflective Judgement must subsume under a law not yet given and therefore serves as its own principle, producing necessary maxims for guiding cognition of natural laws in experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise when you are operating reflectively (seeking principles) vs determinately (applying known laws). Reflective maxims are methodological and may conflict, producing dialectical antinomies that need critical resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antinomy of the Judgement: two conflicting maxims
rubrics_metrics.description: First maxim: all production of material things and their forms must be judged possible according to merely mechanical laws. Second maxim: some products of material nature cannot be judged possible according to merely mechanical laws (require final causes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these as regulative maxims of reflective judgement rather than constitutive propositions. Do mechanical investigation first and only appeal to teleological reflection when mechanical explanation leaves essential features of purposiveness unaccounted for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule for resolving the antinomy methodologically
rubrics_metrics.description: One must not convert these regulative principles into constitutive principles; rather, follow the mechanical maxim in investigation as far as possible, and employ the teleological maxim only as a guide where the mechanical fails to reveal grounds for natural purposiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid dogmatic assertions that some natural products are impossible under mechanism; keep the judgement open and use teleology as a heuristic, not as proof of non-mechanical causality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction of Technic: designed (technica intentionalis) vs undesigned (technica naturalis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Call the procedure of nature according to the rule of purposes 'Technic', and divide it into designed (technica intentionalis) where nature's productive faculty is taken as a particular kind of causality, and undesigned (technica naturalis) where purposiveness is explained subjectively as our mode of judging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When explaining purposiveness, specify whether you treat it as genuinely designed causality (requiring some form of intelligence) or as an appearance arising from mechanistic processes and our judgemental standpoint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systems explaining purposiveness must be critically evaluated (Idealism vs Realism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two broad families: Idealism (purposiveness is undesigned — e.g., Epicurean chance or Spinozan fatality) and Realism (some purposiveness is designed — e.g., Hylozoism or Theism). Each subvariant (casuality/fatality, hylozoism/theism) tries to account for purposiveness but fails to give a satisfactory dogmatic account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid uncritical adoption of systems that either reduce purposiveness to blind chance or assert designed causality beyond what can be established; prefer a critical, regulative use of teleology that recognises limits of our cognitive faculties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit on dogmatic treatment: the concept of a natural purpose is inexplicable a priori
rubrics_metrics.description: To use the concept dogmatically (as a determinant principle) would require assurance of its objective reality; but the concept of a thing as a natural purpose, though empirically conditioned and useful as a rational principle of judgement, cannot be dogmatically established a priori.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat teleological concepts critically: they are allowable as methodological, regulative tools for reflective judgement about empirical objects, but not as proof of metaphysical claims about the world's ultimate causal order.
